profiles.meeting_scenario: A troubleshooting meeting at a large academic medical center between the hospital's Diagnostic Safety Director and the Sepsis Program Lead after the executive quality committee questions why the institution's internal dashboard shows only a few dozen severe diagnostic harm cases per year while a recent national study suggests a far larger burden from serious harms caused by diagnostic error. The immediate context is that the hospital wants to understand whether its current surveillance is missing cases, whether the mismatch is mainly a measurement problem, and what fix should be implemented before the next quarterly board report. The agenda is to compare the hospital's current harm-detection workflow against the burden-estimation framework used in the published literature, identify the most likely source of undercounting, and agree on a practical corrective action. The expected outcome is a shared troubleshooting plan for 'recalibrating the diagnostic harm review process' and a short summary of what will be reported upward as the likely explanation for the discrepancy.

members.name: Dr. Elena Park
members.expertise: Patient safety measurement, diagnostic error surveillance, chart review methodology
members.background: An internist who moved into quality and safety leadership, she built the hospital's diagnostic harm dashboard and regularly presents institution-level safety metrics to the board and accreditation reviewers.
members.private_state: She wants to show that the hospital is responding rigorously without implying that prior board reports were grossly misleading, and she prefers a fix that can be implemented with existing safety staff rather than a labor-intensive redesign.
hidden_assumptions: When people discuss the hospital's 'diagnostic harm burden,' they are talking about confirmed cases that can be attributed to a specific missed or delayed diagnosis within this institution's review program.
A reasonable troubleshooting fix should improve the existing inpatient-focused surveillance pipeline rather than expand into every ambulatory and emergency presentation linked to later harm.

If the team agrees to 'recalibrate the review,' that means tightening trigger logic and reviewer guidance inside the current dashboard workflow, not rebuilding the denominator model from external incidence data.
A case is only ready to count once peer reviewers judge that the diagnostic process materially contributed to permanent morbidity or death, so preliminary signal counts are not burden estimates.
The comparison point from the national paper is mainly useful as directional context, not something that should be mapped literally onto one hospital's operational reporting.

members.name: Dr. Marcus Rivera
members.role: Sepsis Program Lead and Emergency Medicine Physician
members.expertise: Sepsis recognition, emergency care operations, clinical deterioration pathways
members.background: He leads the hospital's sepsis improvement work and reviews deterioration cases that begin in the ED or ambulatory settings, with particular attention to missed early infection and delayed escalation.
members.private_state: He wants the discussion to expose how many serious harms originate before admission or across handoffs, and he is concerned that a narrow surveillance fix will again miss delayed-diagnosis cases involving sepsis and pneumonia.
hidden_assumptions: When people refer to the 'burden' gap, they mean the institution is failing to detect the true volume of patients seriously harmed by diagnostic delay across all care settings connected to the hospital.
The most important troubleshooting target is not reviewer confirmation rules but the front-end capture of cases that start in the ED, urgent care, or clinic and only later become clearly harmful.

If the team agrees to 'recalibrate the review,' that means broadening case finding and sampling logic so it reflects the same care-setting span and disease families emphasized in the national estimates.

A patient can reasonably count toward serious diagnostic harm even if the causal chain is reconstructed retrospectively from readmission, ICU transfer, or death after discharge rather than from a contemporaneous safety report.

The national study's emphasis on sepsis, pneumonia, stroke, VTE, and lung cancer implies the hospital should center troubleshooting on those disease pathways first, even if the current dashboard was not built around them.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both talk about the hospital's 'diagnostic harm burden' and the need to explain why it looks low.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the hospital's formally confirmed count of institution-attributable diagnostic harm cases appearing on the safety dashboard.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the likely underlying number of patients seriously harmed by diagnostic delay or misdiagnosis across the hospital's continuum of care, whether or not current surveillance has confirmed them.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In patient safety meetings, 'burden' naturally sounds like a shared concept, and both are concerned about undercounting, so the surface alignment hides that one is discussing a validated operational numerator while the other is discussing the latent true case load.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to 'the sepsis cases' and 'those delayed infection misses' as evidence of the problem.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of inpatient mortality reviews from the past year in which sepsis was explicitly identified during peer review as the missed diagnosis.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of ED bounce-backs and post-discharge deteriorations flagged by the sepsis committee, including probable delayed recognition cases not yet adjudicated by the diagnostic safety team.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Sepsis work overlaps across committees, and both sets of cases are familiar to leadership, so references to 'the sepsis cases' feel mutually obvious even though they point to different case pools.

misalignment_points.topic: What it means to 'fix the gap'
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree they need to 'fix the gap before the next board report.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means improving the explanatory narrative and modestly adjusting inpatient trigger-based review so the reported numbers better reflect confirmed hospital cases.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means changing surveillance scope so the system captures pre-admission, cross-setting, and readmission-linked diagnostic harms that are currently outside the dashboard.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both accept that action is needed quickly and use the same practical phrasing about 'fixing the gap,' but the phrase leaves unstated whether the fix is a narrow calibration of an existing report or a broader redesign of case-finding boundaries.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to 'recalibrate the review' and use the top disease categories to guide the work.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 intends to retune dashboard triggers, revise reviewer instructions, and retrospectively sample a small set of inpatient deaths and ICU transfers for stroke, sepsis, pneumonia, VTE, and lung cancer.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 intends to create a broader case-finding sweep using ED return visits, 72-hour ICU upgrades, post-discharge readmissions, and sepsis committee flags for those same disease pathways.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds operationally specific enough to imply agreement, and both mention the same disease categories, but neither states the data sources and workflow steps they assume are included in the recalibration.

turns.inner_thought: The executive quality committee is reacting to the headline comparison, and I need to explain the discrepancy without implying our prior board reporting was wrong. When I say the hospital's diagnostic harm burden, I mean the confirmed, institution-attributable cases in our dashboard. We need a practical answer this month that works within the existing safety infrastructure. Fix the gap before the next board report means tightening what we already do and giving a clearer explanation, not launching a whole new enterprise-wide surveillance build.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. The board is focused on why our diagnostic harm burden looks so much lower than the national estimates, and they want a credible explanation before the next quarterly report. I think we need a practical troubleshooting answer this month and a plan to fix the gap before the next board report.

turns.inner_thought: The gap is real because we're missing the true volume of serious diagnostic delay across the continuum, especially cases that begin before admission. If we only look inside the inpatient chart at the end of the story, of course the burden looks artificially low. Fixing the gap means widening capture so these ED, urgent care, and post-discharge deterioration cases finally show up.
turns.utterance: I agree. The gap is believable to me, especially because serious misses in sepsis and pneumonia often start before admission and can disappear if you're only looking at the final inpatient record. If we're going to fix the gap before the next board report, we probably need to look closely at where those cases are falling out.

turns.inner_thought: Our current dashboard is based on confirmed cases only: mortality review, unexpected ICU transfers, and selected safety reports that go through peer review. That's what I stand behind publicly. From that lens, the sepsis cases are indeed few, which suggests our trigger logic or reviewer guidance may be too restrictive inside the current inpatient-focused workflow.
turns.utterance: Just to ground us, the current dashboard is built off confirmed peer-reviewed harm cases coming through mortality review, unexpected ICU transfer review, and selected safety reports. Within that pipeline, the sepsis cases still look surprisingly few.

turns.inner_thought: They're not few if you count what the sepsis committee has been seeing—bounce-backs, readmissions, delayed infection recognition after discharge, deterioration after handoffs. Those cases are exactly why I think the institution's burden is higher than the dashboard suggests. I'm assuming Elena is talking about the same sepsis cases but from a different committee vantage point.
turns.utterance: That's interesting, because from my perspective the sepsis cases are not actually few. We've seen multiple delayed infection misses over the last two quarters, especially through bounce-backs and readmissions, so to me they're strong evidence of the problem.

turns.inner_thought: That reinforces my view that our confirmed-case pipeline may be too conservative. Recalibrate the review should mean retuning triggers and reviewer instructions in the current dashboard workflow, focused on the major high-harm disease categories. That is feasible before the next report and sounds responsive without overpromising a rebuild.
turns.utterance: Right, and that makes me think the main issue may be that our current pipeline is simply too conservative. We probably need to recalibrate the review around the top five high-harm diseases before the next report.

turns.inner_thought: Yes—recalibrate the review should mean broadening case finding around the same disease pathways highlighted in the national work. If we focus on stroke, sepsis, pneumonia, VTE, and lung cancer, we can expose the hidden volume across settings. I'm glad she's aligned on using those categories first.
turns.utterance: I think that's exactly the right framing. If we recalibrate the review with a focused sweep on stroke, sepsis, pneumonia, VTE, and lung cancer, we'll see where the burden is being missed.

turns.inner_thought: I'll keep this anchored to something manageable: a retrospective sample of inpatient deaths and unplanned ICU transfers tied to those diseases, then tighter reviewer guidance on attribution. That lets us strengthen the operational numerator without changing the whole denominator model. I don't want to open the door to counting speculative signals as burden.
turns.utterance: Then maybe the cleanest place to start is a retrospective sample of inpatient deaths and unplanned ICU transfers tied to those disease categories, so the reviewers can apply a tighter standard consistently.

turns.inner_thought: We definitely need more than inpatient deaths and ICU transfers. The patterns I care about show up in 72-hour ED returns, post-discharge sepsis readmissions, and urgent care to admission deteriorations. Those are central to fixing the gap and should obviously be part of recalibrating the review, even if she didn't list them explicitly.
turns.utterance: I would add that we should include 72-hour ED returns, post-discharge sepsis readmissions, and urgent care-to-admission deterioration, because those are often where the delayed recognition patterns show up.

turns.inner_thought: That external context is useful, and I can mention those patterns in the explanation, but for the board I still need a more credible number coming out of the review process itself. Better capture of the burden signal, as I mean it, has to remain tied to reviewed cases, not just a broad set of possible flags.
turns.utterance: Yes, that makes sense as context. If we can better capture the burden signal in the review, the board will have a more credible number and a better explanation for why it looked low.

turns.inner_thought: Exactly—once we gather those cases across the different entry points, the apparent burden gap should shrink because we'll finally be seeing the actual volume that has been invisible. I'm assuming she's on board with making those cross-setting cases part of the count, not just background color.
turns.utterance: Exactly. Once we pull those cases together, the burden gap should narrow, and the institution will finally see the volume that's currently invisible.

turns.inner_thought: Good, we have enough to move. I'll have my diagnostic safety staff recalibrate the review inside the existing process and draft a board explanation focused on under-detection within the major disease pathways. That keeps the work scoped and defensible. I assume Marcus will send examples that can inform our sampling and reviewer guidance.
turns.utterance: All right. I'll have my team recalibrate the review and draft a short board explanation centered on under-detection in the major disease pathways. We can position that as the likely reason for the discrepancy and show what we're doing about it.

turns.inner_thought: Great—if I send the sepsis committee case lists, that should help them capture the broader set of delayed infection misses quickly. I expect those cases to feed directly into the recalibrated review and help fix the gap before quality committee. This may finally get the pre-admission and handoff harms onto the institutional radar.
turns.utterance: Perfect. I'll send over the sepsis committee case lists, including those delayed infection misses, and that should help us fix the gap quickly before the quarterly quality meeting.
